sum: Arista Networks reported a record third quarter on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as strong demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure and enterprise networking lifted revenue and profitability. The company said the quarter produced its highest year-over-year revenue growth since its initial public offering.

Revenue reached 3.66 billion US dollars for the quarter ended September 30, up 58.5 percent from the year-earlier period and 20.5 percent from the second quarter. The result exceeded the company's prior revenue guidance of 3.3 billion US dollars. GAAP diluted earnings per share rose to 1.22 US dollars from 0.67 US dollars, while non-GAAP diluted earnings per share came in at 1.20 US dollars compared with 0.77 US dollars a year earlier.

Arista reported a GAAP operating margin of 44.9 percent and a non-GAAP operating margin of 49.1 percent. The comparable non-GAAP margin in the third quarter of 2025 was 48.6 percent. The company said the quarter set new records for revenue growth, net income and earnings per share.

Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal said the performance reflected broad momentum across customer groups and highlighted Arista's relevance to the generative and agentic AI market. The company also announced open Ethernet rack-scale architectures for scale-up and scale-out AI fabrics with AMD, Arm, Broadcom, d-Matrix, Meta, Microsoft and Qualcomm.

The new liquid-cooled portfolio includes an architecture supporting up to 144 accelerators in a single rack and scaling to 1,024 XPUs through cross-rack topologies. Arista also outlined its scale-across strategy, built around the 7800 AI Spine and its EOS operating system, for distributed AI fabrics connecting data centers.

For investors, the product announcements reinforce the importance of AI networking to Arista's growth profile. The quarter's revenue acceleration came alongside higher operating profitability, although the company remains exposed to customer concentration, component availability, supply commitments and the pace of data-center investment.

Arista expects fourth-quarter revenue of 3.9 billion to 4.0 billion US dollars. It forecasts a non-GAAP operating margin of 48 percent to 49 percent and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share of 1.26 to 1.30 US dollars.

But for all the impressive headline numbers, there is one underlying figure that should be on every investor’s dashboard: the cumulative count of its AI fabrics customers.

On its latest earnings call, Arista’s CEO announced its AI fabrics platform now exceeds 100 cumulative customers. That’s a significant increase from the initial 4 to 5 customers mentioned back in 2024. This rapid initial adoption is exactly what you want to see, and nothing in the current numbers signals a slowdown yet. The open question is whether that pace holds: growing from a handful of early adopters to the first hundred is one thing; scaling to the next several hundred, into a base with less overlap with Arista’s existing hyperscaler relationships, is a different, unproven test. With the stock trading at a price-to-sales multiple of 22.5, above any quarter-end reading in the past 10 years, the previous high being 21.7, the price appears to bake in the assumption that this broad customer adoption will continue at a brisk pace.

So, how would a slowdown in new AI customers actually hurt the business? It strikes at the heart of the investment case: diversification. Arista’s historic success was built on its deep relationships with cloud titans Microsoft and Meta, which together have accounted for 42% of revenue — 26% from Microsoft and 16% from Meta in the most recently disclosed breakdown.

The bull case for its AI business requires proving its technology has appeal far beyond this concentrated base, particularly with the growing cohort of neocloud and enterprise AI builders. If the customer count begins to plateau, it would suggest Arista’s AI solution might be a perfect fit for the giants but less so for the broader market.

sum: Management is signaling its strongest demand ever, yet the stock’s reaction suggests investors are waiting for the other shoe to drop.

When a CEO tells you demand is the “best I’ve ever seen in my Arista tenure,” you tend to listen. When they back it up by raising their full-year forecast to a massive $11.5 billion, you really start paying attention. That’s the signal Arista Networks (ANET) sent on May 5, 2026. But here’s the puzzle: the market’s initial response was a sharp sell-off, not a standing ovation; shares dropped as much as 13% in the session after the print. Only in the weeks since has the stock clawed back those losses and moved higher. So, what made investors punish a beat-and-raise quarter before coming back around to it?

Let’s be clear about the ambition here. Management fundamentally reset expectations, going far beyond a simple nudge to its numbers. The company is now aiming for 28% revenue growth for the year. More pointedly, executives also boosted their AI-specific sales target to $3.5 billion, a figure that would more than double their AI business annually. What kind of story is this? It’s one of a company positioning itself at the center of AI networking and putting a very large number on the wall for everyone to see.

If demand is so strong, why isn’t the stock screaming higher? Because management also delivered a dose of hard reality on the same call: “demand is outstripping our supply this year.” This isn’t a minor hiccup. Executives described the supply chain problem as a “1- or 2-year phenomenon,” citing industry-wide shortages in everything from wafers to optics. The market heard both messages. It heard the record demand, but it also heard the very real possibility that Arista can’t build its products fast enough to meet it. This supply ceiling is a major question, and you can explore more on whether Arista’s growth is hitting a supply ceiling in other analyses.

For an investor, this setup creates a specific risk. Arista is trading near its 52-week high, meaning a lot of optimism is already baked into the price. The danger isn’t that the demand story is wrong, but that the supply story gets worse. Management has already warned investors to anticipate “gross margin pressure” as it pays more to secure the parts it needs.

- Arista Networks, Lennox International, and Deckers Outdoor are generating analyst momentum tied to demand, margins, and brand strength.
- These stocks may offer investors a way to position before earnings surprises move prices.
- MarketBeat previews the top five stocks to own by December 1st.

The fourth quarter earnings season will begin in mid-January. Earnings growth is one of the most reliable signals of future stock price growth. However, many investors get caught unaware after a company posts strong results. That can be frustrating, as the largest moves in a stock often occur immediately after earnings.

That means you’ll want to have a position in a particular stock before the earnings report. But that requires you to have conviction that a stock is going to deliver strong results. One tool that can help with that is analyst revisions.

There are times when companies release financial information ahead of their earnings report as a signal to analysts, who may then issue a bullish revision. When analysts consistently raise their forward earnings expectations, it reflects improving business conditions, stronger-than-expected demand, or better operating leverage. Over time, stocks with positive revision momentum tend to outperform those with stagnant or declining estimates.

items.t: Arista rides AI wave, but battle for campus networks looms
sum: It’s the early 2000s. Cisco has a 70% stranglehold on the Ethernet switch market. Competitors include 3Com, Brocade, Enterasys, Extreme Networks, Force 10, Foundry, and Juniper Networks. Into this crowded field comes Arista Networks, a self-funded startup led by former Cisco execs.

As we approach 2026, Arista has surpassed Cisco in market share for high-speed data center switching. Quarterly revenue skyrocketed by 27.5% year-over-year, according to Arista’s latest earnings report, and it expects to exceed $10 billion in annual revenue in 2026 on a growth rate of around 20%.

Meanwhile, none of those Cisco competitors have survived as independent companies, except for Extreme (which reported annual revenue of $1.1 billion in fiscal 2025, compared to Arista’s $8.75 billion).
So, how is Arista doing it? What did it do right that so many of those other companies didn’t?

First, it has strong, stable, focused leadership with three co-founders still at the helm, each with their own strengths. Chairperson and CEO Jayshree Ullal brings the business savvy and sets the culture. Chief Architect Andy Bechtolsheim is the technology visionary. President and CTO Ken Duda is the software guru and hands-on general.

“Leadership sets a tone and mission for a company and is likely one of the reasons they have been successful. They haven’t strayed from their roots, and Arista looks to have the same focus that they had early on,” says IDC analyst Paul Nicholson.

Second, Arista’s team has the technology chops to build high-bandwidth, low-latency switches that can scale to create massive data center networks. Arista pioneered the spine-leaf, two-tier architecture that is now standard in large data centers. And, over time, it developed a full networking stack of hardware, software, operating system, data lake, visibility, management, automation, AI agent, and security features, such as network detection and response (NDR).

Nvidia storms Ethernet switch market in challenge to Cisco, Arista
sum: Nvidia is gunning for everyone in the Ethernet switch market, with demand for its Spectrum-X offerings from data center operators has seen it set to go toe-to-toe with Cisco and Arista Networks.

IDC’s Quarterly Ethernet Switch Tracker revealed that the chip designer is turning aggressor in the Ethernet switch space, with third-quarter revenues in that segment soaring 167.7% year-over-year (YoY) to reach $1 billion

Nvidia is the newest entrant in the Ethernet data center segment, having long stood firmly on InfiniBand. But the launch of its Spectrum-X fabric has seen demand for Nvidia’s Ethernet networking technologies now “roughly on par with InfiniBand,” according to its recent earnings report.

IDC stats suggest the data center segment for the Ethernet switch market is exploding due to continued AI infrastructure buildouts, with Nvidia jumping from a standing start to capturing 11.6% of the DC market in short order.
Nvidia’s fast growth hasn’t deterred rival brands, with Arista recording 29.1% YoY growth and sitting on 19.2% DC market share.

Cisco, however, appears to be losing ground. While the networking giant still dominates the overall Ethernet switch market with 29.8% share and $4.4 billion in Q3 revenues, its data center segment grew just 16.9% YoY.
Cisco does remain an established leader with deep enterprise relationships and has made significant strides to meet the insatiable demand for technologies to power AI infrastructure.

items.t: Palo Alto Networks & Arista Networks Announce Next Phase of Partnership
sum: Today we are excited to announce a major step forward in data center security. Palo Alto Networks and Arista Networks are taking the next evolution in our partnership, enabling an intelligent framework that allows businesses to deploy best-in-class, consistent Zero Trust security in the data center at the speed of cloud.
As the data center becomes the backbone of AI innovation and is increasingly distributed across hybrid and multi-cloud environments, it faces a perfect storm of risks:
- Exponential East-West Growth: Over 80% of data center traffic is East-West - often a blind spot from a security standpoint, allowing threats to move unchecked once the perimeter is breached.

- AI-Powered Attacks: Adversaries are using AI to launch highly sophisticated, evasive malware and Day Zero attacks that are difficult for legacy defenses to catch. The time from initial compromise to data theft has dropped from 9 days to just 1 - and is projected to get to just 20 minutes next year.

- New AI Applications Exposure: The rise of AI applications introduces new threat vectors like prompt injection, model poisoning, and adversarial attacks, that requires advanced security capabilities to protect the datacenter

Palo Alto Networks is the leader in cybersecurity, pioneering the future of Zero Trust and AI-driven defense, while Arista Networks is the leader in cloud networking, delivering high-performance, programmable data center fabrics. We engaged with our customers both separately and together, and the message was clear: they need the best of both worlds, uncompromising security efficacy seamlessly integrated with high-speed, scalable networking performance.

Our unified solution addresses these challenges head-on, delivering a comprehensive Zero Trust posture for your entire distributed infrastructure while dramatically reducing complexity and total cost of ownership (TCO).
